source_text: Fragmenta in epistulam ad Galatas (in catenis) Gal: Prolog Τοῦ κηρύγματος εἰς τὰ ἔθνη δεχθέντος τινὲς τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς περιτομῆς ἐξιόντες ἔπειθον τὰ ἔθνη ἰουδαΐζειν, καὶ πρώτη περὶ τούτου φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν μὴ ὑποκεῖσθαι νόμῳ, ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ εἰδωλοθύτου καὶ αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ καὶ πορνείας· οὕτω γὰρ ἔδοξε τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι. ἐκράτησε δὲ τὸ νόσημα τοῦτο τῶν Galατῶν συμφώνως ἰουδαΐζειν βουληθέντων. ἐπείσθησαν δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν διαστρεφόντων λεγόντων, ὡς οἱ λοιποὶ ἀπόστολοι οὐ κωλύουσι τοὺς βουλομένους τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον. 299 Gal 1,4 ∆είκνυσιν ὅτι οὐ Μωϋσῆς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τοῦ κόσμου οὐδέ τις τῶν προφητῶν ἄλλος. οὐ δεῖ τοίνυν ἡττᾶσθαι τοῦ μὴ σώσαντος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀποθανόντος. Gal 1,6–7 Εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερον, φησίν· τὸ γὰρ ἡμέτερον εὐαγγέλιον καὶ τὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐκτὸς ὑμᾶς εἶναι βούλεται νόμου. Gal 1,8–10 Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἡ μεῖς; ὅτε ἐκηρύττομεν, πνεύματος ἁγίου δυνάμει ἐκηρύξαμεν· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον οὐ μετανοεῖ. ἐὰν οὖν ἄλλα εἴπωμεν, κατελίπομεν τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. ἔστω οὖν καὶ ὁ κῆρυξ ἀνάθεμα, ἀθετῶν τὸ κήρυγμα. Παρ' ὃ παρελάβετε. οὐκ ἐκήρυξα μὲν ἐγώ, φησίν, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐλάβετε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγὼ ἐκήρυξα, καὶ ὑμεῖς παρελάβετε. οὔτε ἐγὼ μετανοῶ κηρύξας, καὶ ὑμεῖς τηρήσατε ὃ εἰλήφατε. Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην. μέλλων αὐτοὺς ὑπομιμνήσκειν τοῦ ἰδίου εὐαγγελίου, προλαβὼν ἀσφαλίζεται ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν ὅτι θεραπεύει ὑπαγόμενος· ἐπιπλήττει γὰρ νουθετῶν. εἰπὼν δὲ εἰ ἔτι, ἐδήλωσεν ὅτι ἤρεσκε ποτὲ ἀνθρώποις. τίσι δὲ ἤρεσκεν; παρ' ὧν ἔλαβεν ἐπιστολὰς τοὺς εἰς ∆αμασκὸν πιστοὺς κακῶσαι. εἰ οὖν, φησίν, ἤρεσκον ἔτι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις, οὐκ ἂν ἐπίστευσα τῷ Χριστῷ. Gal 1,13 Τίς χρεία τῆς ἐν τῷ Ἰουδαϊσμῷ ἀναστροφῆς ἀλλ' ἵνα δείξῃ, ὅτι οὐ προλήψει δουλεύει ἀλλ' ἀληθείᾳ· οὐ γὰρ μισήσας τὸν νόμον ὑπέδραμε τὴν χάριν–ἐξεδίκει γὰρ αὐτόν–ἀλλ' εὑρὼν τὸ τέλειον ἀπέστη τοῦ νόμου. Νῦν δείκνυσιν ὅτι πλέον τι τῶν περὶ Πέτρον ἔχει· οὐ γὰρ ἐζήλωσαν ἐκεῖνοι ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰουδαϊσμοῦ ἀπειθοῦντες τῷ Χριστιανισμῷ ὡς ἐγώ. 300 μὴ τοίνυν οἰηθῇτε ὅτι μισήσας τὸν νόμον ἦλθον εἰς τὴν χάριν– ἐξεδίκουν γὰρ τὸν νόμον–ἀλλ' εὗρον τὸ τέλειον, καὶ οὐκ ἐξισῶ τὸν νόμον τῇ τελείᾳ χάριτι. Gal 1,16 Οὐ διαβάλλων δὲ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦτό φησιν, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἐστοίχησα θνητῇ σαρκί. Gal 2,16 Εἰ γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται τῶν πόνον φερόντων, ἐκ δὲ πίστεως ὅπου τὸ τῆς εὐκολίας καὶ τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης μέγα, πῶς οὐκ ἀναγκαῖόν φησιν ἐάσαντας νόμον ἀρκεῖσθαι τῇ χάριτι; ἐξ ἔργων νόμου λέγει μὴ δικαιοῦσθαι, οὐκ ἐξ ἐντολῶν· ἡ γὰρ ἐντολὴ δικαιοῖ ἀκουομένη, τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἦν τὸ δυσκατόρθωτον.
thought_title: The Galatian crisis and Paul's gospel
orientation: Eusebius opens his commentary by describing how the Galatian crisis began in Antioch and then defends Paul's gospel against those who distort it.
pass_a_gloss: The preaching to the nations having been received, some of those from the circumcision going out were persuading the nations to judaize, and first about this a dispute appears to have arisen in Antioch, because the apostles wrote not to be subject to the law, but to abstain from idol-sacrifice and blood and what is strangled and sexual immorality; for thus it seemed good to the Holy Spirit. And this disease prevailed over the Galatians, who wished in agreement to judaize. And they were persuaded by those who distort, saying that the other apostles do not hinder those who wish to keep the law. He shows that Moses did not die for the world, nor any other of the prophets. Therefore one must not be overcome by the one who did not save, but by the one who died for us. To another gospel, which is not another, he says; for our gospel and that of the apostles wishes you to be outside the law. Let it be an angel, but why also we? When we were preaching, in the power of the Holy Spirit we preached; and the Holy Spirit does not change his mind. If therefore we say other things, we have abandoned the things of the Spirit. Let therefore even the herald be accursed, setting aside the proclamation. Beyond what you received. I did not preach, he says, and you did not receive, but both I preached and you received. Neither do I change my mind having preached, and you keep what you have received. For now do I persuade men or God? Or do I seek to please men? If still I were pleasing men, a slave of Christ I would not be. About to remind them of his own gospel, having anticipated he secures himself so that they may not think that he is serving by submitting; for he rebukes while admonishing. And having said if still, he showed that he once was pleasing men. And to whom was he pleasing? Those from whom he received letters to harm the faithful in Damascus. If therefore, he says, I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ. What need is there of the conduct in Judaism, except that he may show that he is not enslaved to prejudice but to truth; for not having hated the law he ran to grace—for he was defending it—but having found the perfect thing he departed from the law. Now he shows that he has something more than those around Peter; for those did not zealously defend Judaism by disobeying Christianity as I did. Therefore do not suppose that having hated the law I came to grace—for I was defending the law—but I found the perfect thing, and I do not make the law equal to perfect grace. And he says this not slandering the apostles, but because I did not follow mortal flesh. For if from works no one is justified of those bearing toil, but from faith where the thing of ease and the thing of righteousness is great, how is it not necessary, he says, having left the law to be satisfied with grace? From works of the law he says one is not justified, not from commandments; for the commandment justifies when heard, but the work was the thing hard to achieve.

choices.why: The glossary defines Ἰουδαϊσμός as Judaism; the verb form is best kept as the traditional English 'judaize' to preserve the technical sense of adopting Jewish practices.
Eusebius uses a medical metaphor for the spread of judaizing; 'disease' preserves the metaphor and the negative judgment.
The standard rendering of Paul's anathema formula; 'accursed' preserves the force of the curse.
The word means difficult to accomplish or set right; 'hard to achieve' captures the contrast with the ease of faith.
The middle voice suggests Paul takes precaution for his own position before rebuking; 'secures himself' preserves the reflexive nuance.
The participle suggests Paul is not flattering or yielding to win them over; 'by submitting' captures the sense of giving in.

bible_refs.note: ὑπὲρ τοῦ κόσμου and ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀποθανόντος echo Paul's 'who gave himself for our sins'
Εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερον quotes Paul's 'to another gospel, which is not another'

pass_b_english: When the preaching had been received among the nations, some from the circumcision party went out and persuaded the nations to judaize. The first dispute about this appears to have arisen in Antioch, because the apostles wrote that they should not be subject to the law, but should abstain from idol-sacrifice, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality; for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit. This disease took hold of the Galatians, who willingly agreed to judaize. They were persuaded by those who distort the gospel, who said that the other apostles do not prevent those who wish to keep the law.
He shows that Moses did not die for the world, nor did any other of the prophets. Therefore we must not be mastered by the one who did not save, but by the one who died for us.
"To a different gospel," he says, "which is not another." For our gospel and that of the apostles wants you to be outside the law.

"Even if an angel"—but why also we? When we preached, we preached in the power of the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit does not change his mind. If then we say other things, we have abandoned the things of the Spirit. So let even the herald be anathema if he rejects the proclamation.
"Contrary to what you received." It is not that I preached, he says, and you did not receive; but I preached, and you received. Neither do I repent of having preached, and you—keep what you received.

"Am I now persuading people or God? Or do I seek to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ." Since he is about to remind them of his own gospel, he secures himself in advance so that they will not think he is currying favor because he is being manipulated; for he rebukes while admonishing. By saying "if still," he showed that he once pleased people. Whom did he please? Those from whom he received letters to harm the faithful in Damascus. If then, he says, I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ.

What need is there for his former conduct in Judaism? It is to show that he is not enslaved to prejudice but to truth. For he did not hate the law and run to grace—he was defending it—but he found what is perfect and departed from the law.

Now he shows that he has something more than those around Peter. For they did not burn with zeal for Judaism in disobedience to Christianity, as I did. Do not think, then, that I hated the law and came to grace—I was defending the law—but I found what is perfect, and I do not make the law equal to the perfect grace.
He does not say this to slander the apostles, but because I did not follow mortal flesh.

For if no one is justified by works, which bring toil, but by faith, where there is ease and the greatness of righteousness, how is it not necessary, he says, to leave the law and be content with grace? He says one is not justified by works of the law, not that one is not justified by commandments; for a commandment justifies when it is heard, but the work was what was hard to achieve.

problems.quote: He does not say this to slander the apostles, but because he did not follow mortal flesh.
problems.source_quote: Οὐ διαβάλλων δὲ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦτό φησιν, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἐστοίχησα θνητῇ σαρκί.
problems.why: English adds motive "to slander" not present in Greek; the source says he is not insulting the apostles, not that he says it to slander them.
problems.fix: He says he is not insulting the apostles, but that he has not been bound to mortal flesh.

problems.quote: Beyond what you received
problems.why: Παρ' ὃ means 'contrary to what' or 'in addition to what', not 'beyond what'. The sense is 'contrary to/rather than what you received'.
problems.fix: Contrary to what you received
problems.ruling: ‘παρ’ ὃ’ means ‘instead of/contrary to what’, not spatial ‘beyond’, altering the sense.

problems.quote: He shows that Moses did not die for the world
problems.source_quote: Δείκνυσιν ὅτι οὐ Μωϋσῆς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τοῦ κόσμου
problems.why: The subject of Δείκνυσιν is Paul (from the lemma Gal 1,4), but English 'He' is ambiguous; could be Eusebius or Paul. Given context, Paul is showing this through his words.
problems.fix: Paul shows that Moses did not die for the world
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: but by the one who died for us
problems.why: ἡττᾶσθαι takes genitive, 'be overcome by'; the contrast is between being overcome by the one who didn't save vs. the one who died for us. 'Be overcome by' is strange with the savior; better 'yield to' or 'submit to'.
problems.fix: yield to the one who died for us
problems.ruling: Omits verb ‘be overcome’; Greek says ‘must be overcome by the one who died for us’, not just ‘by the one’.

problems.quote: To another gospel, which is not another, he says
problems.source_quote: Εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερον, φησίν
problems.why: Εἰς here is 'unto/into' as in 'turning to', not 'To' as dative of direction. Paul's phrase is 'to a different gospel'.
problems.fix: To a different gospel, which is not another, he says
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: wants you to be outside the law
problems.why: ἐκτὸς with genitive means 'without, free from', not 'outside' in a spatial sense. 'Outside the law' suggests illegality; 'free from the law' or 'without the law' is better.
problems.fix: wants you to be free from the law
problems.ruling: ‘ἐκτὸς νόμου’ means ‘without the law’, not ‘outside the law’, changing theological meaning.

problems.quote: Let it be an angel—but why also us?
problems.source_quote: Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς;
problems.why: Ἔστω ἄγγελος is 'Let him be an angel' (the one preaching); 'why also us?' means 'why should we (be accursed) too?' The English loses the conditional curse structure.
problems.fix: Let him be an angel—but why should we too be accursed?
problems.ruling: Translates ‘ἔστω ἄγγελος’ as ‘it’, losing that the preacher is called an angel and the conditional curse.

problems.quote: we have abandoned the things of the Spirit
problems.why: κατελίπομεν is 'we left behind/abandoned', but in context it means 'we would be abandoning'. The conditional is lost.
problems.fix: we would be abandoning the things of the Spirit
problems.ruling: Greek conditional ‘if we say other things, we would abandon’, English gives past perfect ‘we have abandoned’.

problems.quote: I did not preach, he says, and you did not receive; but I preached, and you received
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐκήρυξα μὲν ἐγώ, φησίν, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐλάβετε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγὼ ἐκήρυξα, καὶ ὑμεῖς παρελάβετε
problems.why: The οὐ...ἀλλὰ construction is 'not X but Y': 'It is not that I preached and you did not receive; rather, I preached and you received'. English inverts the negation.
problems.fix: It is not that I preached and you did not receive; rather, I preached and you received
problems.ruling: Negation reversed: Greek ‘not that I preached and you did not receive, but …’, English swaps clauses.

problems.quote: I do not change my mind about what I preached
problems.why: οὔτε continues the negation: 'neither do I change my mind about having preached'. The 'neither/nor' connection to 'you keep' is lost.
problems.fix: neither do I change my mind about having preached, nor should you fail to keep what you received
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: he first secures himself
problems.why: ἀσφαλίζεται is middle 'he secures/protects', but object is himself; 'secures himself' is okay but 'takes precautions' or 'protects himself' better. More importantly, 'by submitting' for ὑπαγόμενος—ὑπάγω here is 'going aside/departing' or 'being led away', not 'submitting'.
problems.fix: he first takes precautions so they may not think he is flattering them as he goes on
problems.ruling: ‘ὑπαγόμενος’ means ‘going aside/departing’, not ‘submitting’; translation misstates the action.

problems.quote: he rebukes while admonishing
problems.why: ἐπιπλήττει is 'he rebukes', νουθετῶν is 'admonishing'; but γὰρ gives reason: 'for he rebukes by admonishing' or 'his admonition is a rebuke'. English reverses the relationship.
problems.fix: for his admonition is a rebuke
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: What need is there for his former conduct in Judaism
problems.source_quote: Τίς χρεία τῆς ἐν τῷ Ἰουδαϊσμῷ ἀναστροφῆς
problems.why: Missing 'his' in Greek; 'his former conduct' adds. More seriously, ἀναστροφῆς is 'way of life/conduct', but the question is rhetorical: 'What need was there to mention his conduct in Judaism?' The English loses the rhetorical force.
problems.fix: What need was there to mention his conduct in Judaism
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: they did not burn with zeal for Judaism by disobeying Christianity as I did
problems.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἐζήλωσαν ἐκεῖνοι ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰουδαϊσμοῦ ἀπειθοῦντες τῷ Χριστιανισμῷ ὡς ἐγώ
problems.why: Misread syntax: ἀπειθοῦντες τῷ Χριστιανισμῷ goes with ἐζήλωσαν: 'they did not burn with zeal for Judaism while disobeying Christianity as I did'. But 'by disobeying' suggests means; actually it's concessive/circumstantial: 'disobeying Christianity'. The 'as I did' attaches to the whole clause, not just 'disobeying'.
problems.fix: they did not, in disobedience to Christianity, burn with zeal for Judaism as I did
problems.ruling: Adds causal ‘by’, whereas Greek says ‘they did not burn with zeal … disobeying Christianity as I did’.

problems.quote: I do not make the law equal to perfect grace
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐξισῶ τὸν νόμον τῇ τελείᾳ χάριτι
problems.why: ἐξισῶ is 'I equal/compare', but context is 'I do not equate the law with perfect grace'. 'Make equal to' is awkward; 'equate with' better.
problems.fix: I do not equate the law with perfect grace
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: a commandment justifies when it is heard
problems.why: ἀκουομένη is passive 'when heard', but sense is 'when it is heard/obeyed'. However, 'when it is heard' is literal and correct per Eusebius's point that hearing is easier than doing.
problems.fix: no change needed
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: but the work was hard to achieve
problems.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἦν τὸ δυσκατόρθωτον
problems.why: Missing 'of the law' or context; 'the work' alone is ambiguous. δυσκατόρθωτον is 'hard to accomplish', 'hard to achieve' is fine.
problems.fix: but the work of the law was hard to accomplish
problems.ruling: no ruling

fixed: He does not say this to slander the apostles: source has Οὐ διαβάλλων δὲ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦτό φησιν, 'not slandering the apostles he says this'; English added 'to slander' as motive. Fixed.
Beyond what you received: Παρ' ὃ means 'contrary to what', not 'beyond what'. Fixed.
He shows that Moses did not die for the world: subject is Paul from lemma Gal 1,4. Fixed.
but by the one who died for us: 'be overcome by' is odd with the savior; 'yield to' better. Fixed.
To another gospel: Εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον is 'to a different gospel'. Fixed.
wants you to be outside the law: ἐκτὸς νόμου means 'free from the law'. Fixed.
Let it be an angel—but why also us?: lost conditional curse structure. Fixed.
we have abandoned the things of the Spirit: conditional lost; should be 'would be abandoning'. Fixed.
I did not preach...: negation inverted; fixed to 'It is not that... rather...'.
I do not change my mind...: οὔτε...οὔτε connection lost; fixed.
he first secures himself... by submitting: ὑπαγόμενος is 'going on', not 'submitting'; fixed.
for he rebukes while admonishing: γὰρ gives reason; fixed to 'his admonition is a rebuke'.
What need is there for his former conduct: rhetorical force lost; fixed.
they did not burn with zeal... by disobeying: syntax misread; fixed.
I do not make the law equal to perfect grace: 'equate with' better; fixed.
a commandment justifies when it is heard: no change needed; literal and correct.
but the work was hard to achieve: added 'of the law' for clarity; fixed.

problems.quote: For he did not hate the law and run to grace—for he was defending it—but he found what is perfect and departed from the law.
problems.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ μισήσας τὸν νόμον ὑπέδραμε τὴν χάριν–ἐξεδίκει γὰρ αὐτὸν–ἀλλ' εὑρὼν τὸ τέλειον ἀπέστη τοῦ νόμου.
problems.why: Greek says he proved the law (ἐξεδίκει) after rushing to grace; English says he was defending the law, changing the sense.
problems.fix: For he did not hate the law and rushed to grace—he proved it—but he found what is perfect and departed from the law.

problems.quote: Let him be an angel—but why should we too be accursed?
problems.source_quote: Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς;
problems.why: ἡμεῖς is 'we', not 'we too be accursed'; Paul asks why 'we' should be anathema.
problems.fix: Let him be an angel—but why should we be accursed?
problems.ruling: Greek lacks 'accursed'; adds false meaning

problems.quote: Contrary to what you received
problems.why: Παρ' ὃ means 'besides/what' not 'contrary to'; 'alongside what you received'.
problems.fix: Beyond what you received
problems.ruling: παρ' ὃ means 'besides/apart from', not 'contrary to'

problems.quote: fail to keep
problems.why: τηρήσατε is imperative 'keep!', not 'fail to keep'; negation added.
problems.fix: and you, keep what you received
problems.ruling: τηρήσατε is imperative 'keep!', translation adds negation

problems.quote: he does not serve by prejudice but by truth
problems.why: δουλεύει is 'he serves', but subject is Paul's conduct, not 'he' ambiguous; 'serve' needs object.
problems.fix: he does not serve prejudice but truth
problems.ruling: Adds 'by prejudice' and misrenders οὐ προλήψει

problems.quote: he did not follow mortal flesh
problems.why: ἐστοίχησα is first person 'I did not follow', not 'he'; speaker confused.
problems.fix: I did not follow mortal flesh
problems.ruling: Pronoun mis‑attributed; source is first person

problems.quote: works, which bring toil
problems.why: Relative clause modifies 'works of the law', but 'works' alone loses 'of the law'.
problems.fix: works of the law, which bring toil

previous_english: When the preaching had been received among the Gentiles, some from the circumcision party went out and were persuading the Gentiles to judaize. The first dispute about this appears to have arisen in Antioch, because the apostles had written that they should not be subject to the law, but should abstain from idol-sacrifice, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality; for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit. This disease took hold of the Galatians when they all agreed in wanting to judaize. They were persuaded by those who distort the gospel, who said that the other apostles do not prevent those who wish to keep the law.
Paul shows that Moses did not die for the world, nor did any other of the prophets. Therefore one must not be overcome by the one who did not save, but yield to the one who died for us.
To a different gospel, which is not another, he says. For our gospel and that of the apostles wants you to be outside the law.

Let him be an angel—but why also we? When we preached, we preached in the power of the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit does not change his mind. If then we say other things, we would be abandoning the things of the Spirit. So let even the herald be accursed if he sets aside the proclamation. Contrary to what you received. It is not that I preached, he says, and you did not receive; rather, I preached, and you received. Neither do I change my mind about having preached, and you, keep what you received. For am I now persuading people or God? Or am I seeking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ. Since he is about to remind them of his own gospel, he first takes precautions so that they may not think he is flattering them as he goes on; for his admonition is a rebuke. By saying if still, he made clear that he once pleased people. Whom did he please? Those from whom he received letters to harm the faithful in Damascus. If then, he says, I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ.

What need was there to mention his conduct in Judaism, except to show that he does not serve prejudice but truth? For he did not hate the law and rush to grace—he proved it—but he found what is perfect and departed from the law. Now he shows that he has something more than those around Peter; for they did not, in disobedience to Christianity, burn with zeal for Judaism as I did. Do not think, then, that I hated the law and came to grace—for I was defending the law—but I found what is perfect, and I do not equate the law with perfect grace.
He says this not insulting the apostles, but because he did not conform to mortal flesh.

For if no one is justified from works of the law, which bring toil, but from faith, where there is ease and the greatness of righteousness, how is it not necessary, he says, to leave the law and be content with grace? He says that no one is justified from works of the law, not from commandments; for a commandment justifies when it is heard, but the work of the law is hard to accomplish.
